Part I
:::

[Assume the distribution is known;]{.known} [the sample is unknown.]{.unknown}

# Basic Concepts {.hero #s01-probability}

::: {.sem-mark data-sem="1"}
Counting, sets, conditioning and Bayes
:::

## Probability of an Event {.formula-slide #prob-count}

::: {.lede-min}
Divide the number of outcomes in the event by the total number of possible outcomes.
:::

$$P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) = \frac{\#\ \text{ways } \color{#93C54B}{A} \text{ can happen}}{\#\ \text{of things that can happen}} = \frac{|\color{#93C54B}{A}|}{|\Omega|}$$

:::: {.two-col}
::: {.fragment}
[Flip a coin twice]{.col-head}

$\Omega = \{hh,\ ht,\ th,\ tt\} \quad \color{#6E7681}{\text{4 in all}}$

```{=html}
<div class="coin-row">
<svg width="246" height="34" viewBox="0 0 246 34" aria-label="the four outcomes of two coin flips">
<g font-family="Roboto, sans-serif" font-size="13" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle">
<circle cx="13" cy="17" r="11" fill="rgba(147,197,75,0.18)" stroke="#93C54B" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="13" y="22" fill="#5E8A1E">H</text>
<circle cx="39" cy="17" r="11" fill="rgba(147,197,75,0.18)" stroke="#93C54B" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="39" y="22" fill="#5E8A1E">H</text>
<circle cx="75" cy="17" r="11" fill="rgba(147,197,75,0.18)" stroke="#93C54B" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="75" y="22" fill="#5E8A1E">H</text>
<circle cx="101" cy="17" r="11" fill="none" stroke="#B0B7C0" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="101" y="22" fill="#6E7681">T</text>
<circle cx="137" cy="17" r="11" fill="none" stroke="#B0B7C0" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="137" y="22" fill="#6E7681">T</text>
<circle cx="163" cy="17" r="11" fill="rgba(147,197,75,0.18)" stroke="#93C54B" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="163" y="22" fill="#5E8A1E">H</text>
<circle cx="199" cy="17" r="11" fill="none" stroke="#B0B7C0" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="199" y="22" fill="#6E7681">T</text>
<circle cx="225" cy="17" r="11" fill="none" stroke="#B0B7C0" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="225" y="22" fill="#6E7681">T</text>
</g>
</svg>
</div>
```

[At least one head]{.col-lab}

$\color{#93C54B}{A} = \{hh,\ ht,\ th\} \qquad P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) = \tfrac{3}{4} = 75\%$

[No heads]{.col-lab}

$\color{#325D88}{B} = \{tt\} \qquad P(\color{#325D88}{B}) = \tfrac{1}{4} = 25\%$
:::

::: {.fragment}
[Roll two dice]{.col-head}

::: {.dice-grid}
<div id="dicegrid-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

$\Omega = \{11,\ 12,\ \ldots,\ 66\} \quad \color{#6E7681}{\text{36 in all}}$

[At least one five]{.col-lab}

$\color{#93C54B}{A} = \{15, 25, 35, 45, 51, 52, 53, 54, 55, 56, 65\}$

$P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) = \tfrac{11}{36}$

[Or split on the first die]{.col-lab}

$P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) = \tfrac{1}{6} + \tfrac{5}{6} \times \tfrac{1}{6} = \tfrac{6}{36} + \tfrac{5}{36} = \tfrac{11}{36}$
:::
::::

::: {.pitfall .fragment}
Adding 6 + 6 = 12 counts the outcome (5, 5) twice. In the calculation on the right, the second case excludes a five on the first die, so the cases do not overlap.
:::

## Combinatorics and the Factorial {.formula-slide #combinatorics}

::: {.lede-min}
There are $n$ choices and you are taking $r$ of them. The formula depends on whether you sample with replacement and whether order matters.
:::

$$n! = n \times (n-1) \times \cdots \times 2 \times 1 \qquad 0! = 1$$

::::: {.three-col}
::: {.fragment}
[With replacement]{.col-head}
[Order matters]{.col-sub}

$$n^{\,r}$$

[Ten coin flips in a row]{.col-lab}

$2^{10} = 1{,}024$
:::

::: {.fragment}
[Without replacement]{.col-head}
[Order matters]{.col-sub}
[Permutation · $^{n}P_{r}$]{.col-term}

$$\dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}$$

[Five cards off the top of the deck]{.col-lab}

$\begin{array}{@{}r@{\;}c@{\;}l@{}}
\dfrac{52!}{47!} & = & 52 \times 51 \times 50 \times 49 \times 48 \\[3pt]
 & = & 311{,}875{,}200
\end{array}$
:::

::: {.fragment}
[Without replacement]{.col-head}
[Order does not matter]{.col-sub}
[Combination · $^{n}C_{r}$]{.col-term}

$$\dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!\,r!} = \dbinom{n}{r}$$

[Different orders of the same hand]{.col-lab}

::: {.stack}
```{=html}
<div class="perm-row"><span>K Q 2 3 7</span><span>K 2 Q 7 3</span></div>
```

$\dbinom{52}{5} = 2{,}598{,}960$
:::
:::
:::::

::: {.note-box .fragment}
The last two formulas differ by $r!$, the number of possible orders of the $r$ selected items. There are 311,875,200 ordered deals and 2,598,960 hands, because each hand can be dealt in $5! = 120$ ways.
:::

## Choosing Without Order {.ojs-slide .example #choose-count}

::: {.lede-min}
How many selections are possible? Order does not matter in these four examples, so each uses combinations of $r$ items from $n$.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Exercise 5 of the 2026-27 sheet (Seminar 4 in the 2025-26 beamer):
// 6C3 = 20, 10C3 = 120, 8C4 = 70, 5C2 x 3C2 = 30.
chCases = [
  {q: "6 shirts, pack 3", groups: [{tag: "T", n: 6, r: 3}], what: "T-shirts"},
  {q: "10 people, call 3", groups: [{tag: "P", n: 10, r: 3}], what: "people to call"},
  {q: "8 friends, invite 4", groups: [{tag: "F", n: 8, r: 4}], what: "friends"},
  {q: "2 men + 2 women", groups: [{tag: "M", n: 5, r: 2}, {tag: "W", n: 3, r: 2}], what: "guests"}
]
viewof chIn = Inputs.form({
  q: Inputs.radio(chCases.map(d => d.q), {value: chCases[0].q, label: "Question"}),
  again: Inputs.button("Another pick")
}, {template: ins => html`<div class="cl-dials">${ins.q}${ins.again}</div>`})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
chCase = chCases.find(d => d.q === chIn.q)
chC = (n, r) => { let c = 1; for (let k = 1; k <= r; k++) c = c * (n - r + k) / k; return c; }
chPick = { chIn.again;   // a fresh random pick on every press
  return chCase.groups.map(g => new Set(d3.shuffle(d3.range(g.n)).slice(0, g.r))); }
chFact = (n, r) => d3.range(n, n - r, -1).join(" × ")
chTotal = chCase.groups.reduce((t, g) => t * chC(g.n, g.r), 1)
{
  const rows = chCase.groups.map((g, gi) => html`<div class="ch-row">${d3.range(g.n).map(i =>
    html`<span class="ch-chip ${chPick[gi].has(i) ? "on" : ""}">${g.tag}${i + 1}</span>`)}</div>`);
  const one = g => html`<sup>${g.n}</sup>C<sub>${g.r}</sub> = ${g.n}! / (${g.r}! · ${g.n - g.r}!) = (${chFact(g.n, g.r)}) / (${chFact(g.r, g.r)}) = <b>${chC(g.n, g.r)}</b>`;
  const eq = chCase.groups.length === 1 ? one(chCase.groups[0])
    : html`<sup>5</sup>C<sub>2</sub> × <sup>3</sup>C<sub>2</sub> = ${chC(5, 2)} × ${chC(3, 2)} = <b>${chTotal}</b>`;
  const fb = chCase.groups.length === 1
    ? html`The selection shown is <b>one of ${chTotal}</b>. Press <b>Another pick</b> to choose different ${chCase.what}. Dividing by ${chCase.groups[0].r}! accounts for the possible orders of each selection.`
    : html`Choose the men and the women <b>separately, then multiply</b>: each of the ${chC(5, 2)} pairs of men can go with each of the ${chC(3, 2)} pairs of women, so ${chC(5, 2)} × ${chC(3, 2)} = ${chTotal}.`;
  return html`<div class="ch-wrap">${rows}<div class="ojs-eq ch-eq">${eq}</div><div class="quiz-fb">${fb}</div></div>`;
}
```

## Sample Spaces and Events {.stage-slide #space-intuition}

::: {.lede-min}
The board shows all possible outcomes of rolling two dice. Together they form the sample space $\Omega$. An event is a subset of these outcomes.
:::

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-std}
<div id="space-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="space-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="space-frag-2"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="space-frag-3"}

::: {.slide-footer}
When outcomes are equally likely, calculate probability as a ratio of counts. $P(\color{#93C54B}{A})$ is the cells in $\color{#93C54B}{A}$ over the cells in $\Omega$. That assumption holds for two fair dice, but often fails in real problems.
:::

## Unions, Intersections and Complements {.stage-slide #setops-intuition}

::: {.lede-min}
The board shows two events, $\color{#93C54B}{A}$ and $\color{#325D88}{B}$. Their union $\color{#93C54B}{A} \cup \color{#325D88}{B}$ is "either", their intersection $\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B}$ is "both", and the complement $\color{#93C54B}{A}^{c}$ is every outcome left over.
:::

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-std}
<div id="setops-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="setops-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="setops-frag-2"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="setops-frag-3"}

::: {.slide-footer}
Add 6 and 18 and you get 24, which is three too many. The cells in both events were counted twice, so subtract them once.
:::

## Venn diagrams {.stage-slide #venn-intuition}

::: {.lede-min}
A Venn diagram shows the same events as regions inside circles. The four regions contain the same counts as the board, totalling 36.
:::

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-std}
<div id="venn-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="venn-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="venn-frag-2"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="venn-frag-3"}

::: {.slide-footer}
These circles are drawn to scale, so $\color{#325D88}{B}$ covers three times the area of $\color{#93C54B}{A}$. Most are not, which is why the counts written on them matter more than the picture.
:::

## Set Notation for Probability {.formula-slide #set-formal}

::: {.lede-min}
Counting gives $P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) = |\color{#93C54B}{A}|/|\Omega|$ and $P(\color{#93C54B}{A}^{c}) = 1 - P(\color{#93C54B}{A})$. For unions and intersections, use the following rules.
:::

:::: {.fragment}
::: {.rule-label .rule-or}
[Either]{.rw} · $\color{#93C54B}{A} \cup \color{#325D88}{B}$
:::

$$\begin{array}{@{}l@{\;\;}c@{\;\;}l@{}}
P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cup \color{#325D88}{B}) & = & P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) + P(\color{#325D88}{B}) - P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B})\\[4pt]
\phantom{P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B})} & = & P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) + P(\color{#325D88}{B}) \qquad \color{#6E7681}{\text{if mutually exclusive}}
\end{array}$$
::::

:::: {.fragment}
::: {.rule-label .rule-and}
[Both]{.rw} · $\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B}$
:::

$$\begin{array}{@{}l@{\;\;}c@{\;\;}l@{}}
P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B}) & = & P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) \times P(\color{#325D88}{B} \mid \color{#93C54B}{A})\\[4pt]
\phantom{P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B})} & = & P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) \times P(\color{#325D88}{B}) \qquad \color{#6E7681}{\text{if independent}}
\end{array}$$
::::

::: {.slide-footer .fragment}
Mutually exclusive means $\color{#93C54B}{A} \cap \color{#325D88}{B} = \varnothing$, so there is nothing to subtract. Independent means learning $\color{#93C54B}{A}$ tells you nothing about $\color{#325D88}{B}$, as the conditional probability formula shows.
:::

## Conditional Probabilities {.formula-slide #conditional-probabilities}

::: {.lede-min}
Given that $\color{#325D88}{B}$ occurred, restrict the sample space to its outcomes. The conditional probability is the proportion of those outcomes that also belong to $\color{#93C54B}{A}$.
:::

::: {.cond-row}

:::

Five outcomes remain, and one has a three on the first die, so $P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \mid \color{#325D88}{C}) = \tfrac{1}{5}$. The total tells you something about the first die.
:::
::::

::: {.note-box .fragment}
Here $\color{#93C54B}{A}$ is "the first die is a three". Reversing the conditioning gives a different question, which Bayes' theorem answers.
:::

## Conditioning Narrows the Sample Space {.stage-slide #cond-intuition}

::: {.lede-min}
Eight in ten office managers would buy the software ($\color{#325D88}{A}$), and four in ten of those would also upgrade ($\color{#F47C3C}{B}$). Of the rest, one in ten would. Given $\color{#F47C3C}{B}$, how likely is $\color{#325D88}{A}$?
:::

::: {.stage-wrap .stage-wrap-std}
<div id="cond-stage" class="stage"></div>
:::

[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="cond-frag-1"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="cond-frag-2"}
[]{.fragment .fi-frag id="cond-frag-3"}

::: {.slide-footer .fragment}
Conditioning on $\color{#F47C3C}{B}$ excludes the other 66%, so $P(\color{#325D88}{A} \mid \color{#F47C3C}{B}) = P(\color{#325D88}{A} \cap \color{#F47C3C}{B})/P(\color{#F47C3C}{B})$.
:::

## Reading a Two-Way Table {.ojs-slide .example #table-cond}

::: {.lede-min}
Choose an event and a condition. The table marks the cells used in the numerator and denominator of the probability.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Exercise 4 of the beamer Seminar 3: 1,500 students by sex and course.
ctCols = ["Accountancy", "Economics", "Finance", "Business Info"]
ctRows = ["Male", "Female"]
ctN = [[330, 360, 90, 120], [120, 390, 60, 30]]
ctTotal = 1500
// The cells an event covers, keyed "row,col".
ctCells = ev => new Set(ctRows.includes(ev)
  ? ctCols.map((_, j) => `${ctRows.indexOf(ev)},${j}`)
  : ctRows.map((_, i) => `${i},${ctCols.indexOf(ev)}`))
ctCount = s => [...s].reduce((t, k) => {
  const [i, j] = k.split(",").map(Number);
  return t + ctN[i][j];
}, 0)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof ctA = Inputs.radio([...ctRows, ...ctCols],
  {value: "Economics", label: "Probability of"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof ctB = Inputs.radio(["Nothing", ...ctRows, ...ctCols],
  {value: "Female", label: "Given"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
ctView = {
  const A = ctCells(ctA);
  const B = ctB === "Nothing" ? null : ctCells(ctB);
  const top = B ? new Set([...A].filter(k => B.has(k))) : A;
  const num = ctCount(top), den = B ? ctCount(B) : ctTotal;
  // Navy marks what you divide by; orange, the deck's "the part you want",
  // marks what goes on top. A cell can be both.
  const cls = (i, j) => {
    const k = `${i},${j}`;
    return [top.has(k) ? "ct-top" : "", (!B || B.has(k)) ? "ct-den" : ""].join(" ");
  };
  const rowSum = i => ctN[i].reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
  const colSum = j => ctN[0][j] + ctN[1][j];
  const f3 = v => v.toFixed(3);
  const lhs = B ? `P(${ctA} | ${ctB})` : `P(${ctA})`;
  let verdict;
  if (!B) {
    verdict = html`Nothing is given, so you divide by all ${ctTotal} students.`;
  } else if (num === 0) {
    verdict = html`No student is both. The two events are <b>mutually exclusive</b>, so knowing one rules the other out.`;
  } else if (ctA === ctB) {
    verdict = html`Told it happened, it is certain.`;
  } else {
    const pA = ctCount(A) / ctTotal;
    const same = Math.abs(num / den - pA) < 0.0005;
    verdict = html`Without the condition, P(${ctA}) = ${ctCount(A)} / ${ctTotal} = ${f3(pA)}.
      ${same ? html`The same, so the two are <b>independent</b>.`
             : html`Knowing ${ctB} changes it, so the two are <b>not independent</b>.`}`;
  }
  return html`<div class="ct-wrap">
    <table class="ct-table">
      <thead><tr><th></th>${ctCols.map(c => html`<th>${c}</th>`)}<th class="ct-sum">Total</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody>
        ${ctRows.map((r, i) => html`<tr><th>${r}</th>
          ${ctCols.map((_, j) => html`<td class=${cls(i, j)}>${ctN[i][j]}</td>`)}
          <td class="ct-sum">${rowSum(i)}</td></tr>`)}
        <tr class="ct-sum"><th>Total</th>${ctCols.map((_, j) => html`<td>${colSum(j)}</td>`)}<td>${ctTotal}</td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
    <div class="ct-eq">${lhs} = <span class="ct-num">${num}</span> / <span class="ct-dnm">${den}</span> = ${f3(num / den)}</div>
    <div class="quiz-fb">${verdict}</div>
  </div>`;
}
```

## Independence of taxi breakdowns {.ojs-slide .example #taxi-indep}

::: {.lede-min}
Each taxi has an independent chance of breaking down, so multiply the individual probabilities to find the probability of a particular combination. Set the rates, then put the two old taxis in the same garage.
:::

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof txOld = Inputs.range([0.01, 0.5], {value: 0.10, step: 0.01, format: v => v.toFixed(2), label: "Old taxi breaks down"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof txNew = Inputs.range([0.01, 0.5], {value: 0.05, step: 0.01, format: v => v.toFixed(2), label: "New taxi breaks down"})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof txShared = Inputs.toggle({label: "Old pair share a garage", value: false})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// Exercise 3 of the beamer Seminar 3. A million simulated days, redrawn on
// every change. With the garage shared, the second old taxi breaks down
// exactly when the first does, which is the simplest dependence there is.
txDays = 1000000
txSim = {
  let all4 = 0, newOnly = 0;
  for (let d = 0; d < txDays; d++) {
    const o1 = Math.random() < txOld;
    const o2 = txShared ? o1 : Math.random() < txOld;
    const n1 = Math.random() < txNew, n2 = Math.random() < txNew;
    if (o1 && o2 && n1 && n2) all4++;
    if (!o1 && !o2 && n1 && n2) newOnly++;
  }
  return {all4: all4 / txDays, newOnly: newOnly / txDays};
}
txRule = ({all4: txOld * txOld * txNew * txNew,
           newOnly: (1 - txOld) * (1 - txOld) * txNew * txNew})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const g = v => v.toFixed(6);   // one width for every cell, 0.000025 needs six
  const o = txOld.toFixed(2), n = txNew.toFixed(2), q = (1 - txOld).toFixed(2);
  const verdict = txShared
    ? html`The second old taxi now has the same breakdown outcome as the first. The simulated probability is about <b>${(1 / txOld).toFixed(0)} times</b> the product of the four individual probabilities. Multiplying those probabilities requires <b>independence</b>, which is why the worksheet asks you to state this assumption.`
    : html`The product and simulation agree within sampling variation over a million days. The breakdowns are independent, so their individual probabilities can be multiplied.`;
  return html`<div class="ct-wrap">
    <table class="ct-table">
      <thead><tr><th></th><th>Product rule</th><th>${d3.format(",")(txDays)} days simulated</th></tr></thead>
      <tbody>
        <tr><th>All four break down</th><td>${o} × ${o} × ${n} × ${n} = ${g(txRule.all4)}</td><td class=${txShared ? "ct-top" : ""}>${g(txSim.all4)}</td></tr>
        <tr><th>Only the new ones break down</th><td>${q} × ${q} × ${n} × ${n} = ${g(txRule.newOnly)}</td><td class=${txShared ? "ct-top" : ""}>${g(txSim.newOnly)}</td></tr>
      </tbody>
    </table>
    <div class="quiz-fb ${txShared ? "quiz-no" : "quiz-ok"}">${verdict}</div>
  </div>`;
}
```

$$P(\color{#93C54B}{A}) = \sum_{i} P(\color{#93C54B}{A} \mid \color{#325D88}{B_i})\, P(\color{#325D88}{B_i})$$
:::

:::: {.three-col}
::: {.fragment}
[Supplier 1]{.col-head}
[Half the parts, two per hundred faulty]{.col-sub}

$$0.50 \times 0.02 = 0.010$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
[Supplier 2]{.col-head}
[Three parts in ten, four per hundred faulty]{.col-sub}

$$0.30 \times 0.04 = 0.012$$
:::

::: {.fragment}
[Supplier 3]{.col-head}
[One part in five, seven per hundred faulty]{.col-sub}

$$0.20 \times 0.07 = 0.014$$
:::
::::

::: {.note-box .fragment}
Adding the three routes gives $P(\text{faulty}) = 0.036$. To find the probability that a faulty part came from a particular supplier, use Bayes' theorem.
:::

The base rate gives the relative frequency of each occupation before considering Steve's description. The description is four times as likely for a librarian, while farmers are twenty times as common. Steve is therefore five times as likely to be a farmer.

## Changing the prior probability {.sim-slide #bayes-sim}

::: {.slide-kicker}
Effect of the prior probability
:::

::: {.sim-card .sim-text}
```{webr-r}
prior <- 1 / 21 # <-- P(librarian)
n <- 300000

lib  <- runif(n) < prior

# fits 40% of librarians, 10% of farmers
fits <- runif(n) < ifelse(lib, 0.40, 0.10)

c("P(H)" = prior, "P(H|E)" = mean(lib[fits]))
```
:::

::: {.try-this}
The evidence stays the same as you change the prior. `1/21` corresponds to one librarian for every twenty farmers; at `0.50` you get 0.80. The base rate supplies the relative frequency of the two occupations.
:::
